0.0.n: Introduces a new topic or moves the explanation forward.

0.2.n: Points back to the person already being discussed.

0.3.n: A historical name and title; 推古 is her name, and 天皇 is the imperial title.

0.4.n: The polite form used before が to introduce the topic.

0.5.n: After です, this gently introduces background rather than expressing a strong contrast.

1.0.n: Combines with 史上初 to specify Japanese history.

1.1.n: 史上 means in history, and 初 indicates the first occurrence.

1.2.n: Links 日本史上初 to 女性天皇, describing her as the first such ruler in Japanese history.

1.3.n: Describes 天皇 and forms a phrase for a woman holding the imperial title.

1.4.n: The Japanese sovereign's title applies to women too; Empress is the natural English title here.

1.5.n: Marks the status for which she is famous.

1.6.n: Describes her reputation and takes です to complete the polite statement.

1.7.n: Politely completes the description 有名.

2.0.n: Refers to information beyond the fact just mentioned.

2.1.n: After その他, に helps introduce an additional point.

2.2.n: Adds emphasis that there is another noteworthy fact.

2.3.n: Describes こと and therefore needs な before it.

2.4.n: な connects the describing word 有名 to the noun こと.

2.5.n: A general noun for a matter or piece of information.

2.6.n: Presents what follows as an example of a well-known fact.

2.7.n: Makes 有名なこととして the topic of the following explanation.

2.9.n: A historical person's name and title; 皇子 means an emperor's son.

2.11.n: Introduces the better-known name of the same person.

2.12.n: A historical name and title referring here to the same person as 厩戸皇子.

2.13.n: Identifies Prince Shotoku as the person who served as regent.

2.14.n: Names an official who governs on behalf of a sovereign.

2.15.n: Marks 摂政 as the position held with the verb 務める.

2.16.n: The plain past form of 務める, used for holding a position or fulfilling a role.

3.0.n: Connects the preceding statement to こと, presenting its content as a fact.

3.1.n: Turns the preceding statement into something that can be cited.

3.2.n: Shows that this fact joins the earlier point as another example.

3.3.n: Polite form of 挙げられる, from 挙げる; here it means a fact can be offered as an example.

4.0.n: Refers back to the prince just introduced.

4.1.n: The same historical person's name and title mentioned in the previous sentence.

4.2.n: Marks Prince Umayado as the topic being explained.

4.3.n: Identifies him as belonging to the imperial family.

4.5.n: Introduces a simpler explanation of 皇族.

4.6.n: Refers to the sovereign whose family relationship is being explained.

4.7.n: Connects 天皇 to 親族 to express a family relationship.

4.8.n: A general family term that does not specify the exact relationship.

4.9.n: Politely completes the explanation; Japanese uses present form here when describing historical identity.

4.10.n: Gently invites the listener to share or acknowledge the explanation.

5.0.n: Points back to Prince Umayado, who is already under discussion.

5.1.n: A historical person's name and title, identifying who established the systems in this account.

5.2.n: Identifies the person responsible for the action in this passive sentence.

5.3.n: 制定する becomes 制定される in the passive, then 制定された in the past.

5.4.n: Turns 制定された into a noun phrase meaning the things that were established.

5.5.n: Marks the preceding noun phrase, whose identity is revealed by the names that follow.

5.6.n: Part of the system's name; official ranks were distinguished by caps.

5.7.n: Combines with 二 to make 十二, twelve, within the system's name.

5.8.n: This split belongs to 十二階 as a whole, meaning twelve levels rather than two here.

5.9.n: Joins the names of the two things established.

5.10.n: Combines with 七 to make 十七, seventeen, in the constitution's name.

5.11.n: This split belongs to 十七条 as a whole; 条 counts legal articles, making seventeen articles here.

5.12.n: Links the article count 十七条 to 憲法.

5.13.n: Part of the historical title Seventeen-Article Constitution, not a modern national constitution.

5.14.n: Politely completes the identification of the two things established.

0.lit: Now, as for this Empress Suiko,
0.tip: ですが can introduce a topic gently without meaning but.

1.lit: She is famous as Japan's first female emperor in history.
1.tip: として marks the role or status someone is known for.

2.lit: Besides that, as another well-known fact, Prince Umayado, in other words Prince Shotoku, served as regent,
2.tip: The sentence continues into the next line; つまり identifies two names for the same person.

3.lit: The fact that he did so can also be cited.
3.tip: ということ packages the preceding statement as a fact that the speaker can discuss.

4.lit: This Prince Umayado is an imperial family member, in other words a relative of the emperor, you see.
4.tip: つまり restates a term in simpler words, explaining 皇族 as 天皇の親族.

5.lit: What was established by this Prince Umayado are the Twelve-Level Cap Rank System and the Constitution of Seventeen Articles.
5.tip: 制定されたのが…です means what was established is…, with the answer placed at the end.
